::: {.lead}
A small studio makes a running game called *Tap Runner*. The player taps the
screen, and the character jumps. The studio wants the game on Android phones,
on iPhones and on Windows PCs. To do this, the team must know what happens
inside a device when the player taps, how the processor runs the game, and who
sells the game to the players. In this lesson you learn the main parts of a
computing system and what each part does in a game. You also learn what a
digital platform is, and on which classes of devices people play. Every section ends with a short task that you do on
your phone, on the lab computer or in a mini-game.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary computing-system hardware software cpu memory storage input output instruction-cycle clock-rate digital-platform cloud-gaming >}}

## 1.1 What a game needs from a computer

A phone, a laptop and a game console look very different. Inside, they work in
the same way. Each one is a **computing system**.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.1 — Computing system"}
A **computing system** is a combination of **hardware** (the physical parts),
**software** (the programs) and **data**. It does four jobs: it takes
**input**, it **processes** the input, it **stores** data, and it gives
**output**.
:::

Four main parts do these jobs (@fig-von-neumann):

- the **CPU** (processor) runs the instructions of the programs;
- the **main memory (RAM)** holds the programs and data that are running now.
  It is fast, but it loses everything when the power is off;
- **storage** (flash memory or a disk) keeps apps and files when the power is
  off;
- **input and output devices**: the touch screen, the speaker, the display,
  the buttons.

The parts send data to each other over shared connections called the **bus**.

![The main parts of a computer. The CPU, the main memory and the input/output devices exchange data over the bus.](images/von-neumann.png){#fig-von-neumann width=86%}

One important idea makes all of this work: the program is stored in memory,
in the same way as data. To run a different game, the device only loads a
different program into memory. This is why one phone can run thousands of
different games.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.1 — One tap, four jobs"}
In *Tap Runner*, the player taps the screen to jump.

1. **Input:** the touch screen finds the finger and sends its position.
2. **Processing:** the CPU runs the game's instructions: *is the character on
   the ground? Then start the jump.*
3. **Output:** the new picture appears on the display, and the speaker plays
   the jump sound.
4. **Storage:** at the end of the run, the best distance is saved in storage,
   so it is still there tomorrow.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Memory and storage are the same." They are not. A phone with 8 GB of memory
and 256 GB of storage has 8 GB of fast RAM for the apps that are running, and
256 GB of storage for installed apps and files. Installing many games fills
the storage. Running many games at the same time fills the memory.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Four jobs in your game"}
Choose a game on your phone and play it for one minute.

1. Draw a table with four rows: input, processing, output, storage.
2. In each row, write one thing that happened in your game. For example:
   "Input: I swiped left."

*Your result:* the table with four game events.

::: {.check}
A good table has one real thing from your game in each row, for example:
input: a tap or a swipe; processing: the game decides if you hit an enemy;
output: the picture and the sound; storage: your level or best score after a
restart.
:::
:::

## 1.2 How the CPU runs a game

A game is a long list of very simple **instructions**, such as *add two
numbers* or *compare two numbers*. The CPU runs them one after another, very
fast. For each instruction, it repeats the same three steps (@fig-cycle).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.2 — The instruction cycle"}
The CPU runs a program by repeating the **instruction cycle**:

1. **fetch:** get the next instruction from memory;
2. **decode:** find out what the instruction asks for;
3. **execute:** do it, for example add two numbers, and keep the result.

A clock sets the speed of this cycle. The **clock rate** is measured in
gigahertz (GHz): 3 GHz means 3 billion clock ticks per second.
:::

![The instruction cycle. The CPU repeats it billions of times per second.](images/instruction-cycle.png){#fig-cycle width=62%}

A game draws a new picture, a **frame**, many times per second, for example 60
times. So the CPU must do all the work for one picture in a very short time:
read the touch, move the characters, check if they hit something.

The mini-game below is a version of *Tap Runner*. It shows which part of the
computer works at each moment of a frame.

{{< sim file="sims/one-frame.html" poster="sims/one-frame.png" title="Tap Runner: inside one frame" kind="game" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Watch one frame"}
Open the **Tap Runner** mini-game above (or scan its QR code). Turn on slow
motion.

1. Tap to jump, and watch the parts that light up.
2. Write the parts in the order in which they work during your jump.

*Your result:* the list of parts in order, and one sentence: which part
decides that the character jumps?

::: {.check}
The touch screen (input), then the CPU, then the screen (output). The CPU
decides that the character jumps: it runs the game's instructions.
:::
:::

## 1.3 Digital platforms: where games run and are sold

For a player, "the platform" is the device in their hands. For a game studio,
a platform is more: it decides how the game is made, tested and sold.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.3 — Digital platform"}
A **digital platform** is a combination of a family of devices, an operating
system, development tools, and a store with its own rules. Games are built,
sold and run on it.
:::

![The four layers of a digital platform.](images/platform-stack.png){#fig-stack width=62%}

| Platform | Devices | Operating system | Store |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android | phones and tablets of many makers | Android | Google Play (and others) |
| iOS | iPhone, iPad | iOS, iPadOS | App Store |
| PC | Windows computers of many makers | Windows | Steam, Epic Games Store, … |
| Consoles | PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch | the console maker's system | the console maker's store |

: Main game platforms. {#tbl-platforms}

The owner of a platform makes the rules. It decides what a game may contain,
how players pay, and how much of each sale it keeps. Some platforms check
every game before it can appear in the store. Mobile is the biggest part of
the games market today, with about half of all game revenue. This is why this
diploma focuses on Android and iOS.

Studios do not write a new game for each platform. They use a
**cross-platform** game engine. From one project, the engine makes a separate
version of the game, a **build**, for each platform. The processors are
different too: phones use ARM processors, and most Windows PCs use x86
processors, so a phone build cannot run on a PC. But
the differences do not disappear. Android alone runs on thousands of phone
models with different processors and screens, so a game must be tested on
many of them.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.2 — Bringing a phone game to a console"}
A studio has a puzzle game on Android and iOS. Now it wants the game on the
Nintendo Switch. What changes?

1. **Processor:** the Switch uses an ARM processor, like a phone, and the
   engine makes a new build for it.
2. **Input:** the player also uses buttons and sticks, not only touch.
3. **Output:** the TV screen is big and wide. The phone layout must change.
4. **Rules:** the studio needs an agreement with the console maker, and the
   game must pass the console maker's check before release.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"The platform is just the phone." A platform also includes the operating
system, the tools and the store. The same phone hardware with a different
store or system would be a different platform for a studio.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Platforms at home"}
Think of three devices in your home that can run games (yours or your
family's), for example a phone, a laptop and a console.

1. Draw a table with four columns: device, platform, operating system, store.
2. Fill one row for each device.

*Your result:* the table, and one sentence: which platform is the most common
in your table?

::: {.check}
A good table has three rows, for example: phone, Android, Android, Google
Play; laptop, PC, Windows, Steam; console, PlayStation, the console's
system, PlayStation Store. For most students the phone is the most common.
:::
:::

## 1.4 Device classes for gaming

Students play on very different devices (@fig-devices). @tbl-devices compares
them on the things that matter for a game designer.

![The five device classes on which students play.](images/devices.png){#fig-devices width=92%}

| Property | Smartphone | Tablet | PC / laptop | Console | Cloud gaming |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Input | touch, sensors | touch, sensors | keyboard, mouse, gamepad | gamepad | depends on the device |
| Screen | small | medium | large | TV | any |
| Power | battery, no fan | battery, no fan | mains, fans | mains, fans | the server |
| Play time | short, anywhere | short to medium | long, at a desk | long, at home | needs a fast network |

: Device classes compared for gaming. {#tbl-devices}

A game made for one class must change for another. A touch interface does not
work with a gamepad. A long open-world game does not fit a five-minute bus
ride. A game that needs a fan cannot keep its frame rate on a phone. So the
first question in planning a game, and in testing it, is: *on which devices
will people play it?*

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"A fast phone can run any PC game." Even a fast phone has a small touch
screen, a battery and no fan. The game must still be changed for the phone.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The right device for a game"}
Choose one game that you know well.

1. Write the input it needs (touch, buttons, keyboard…), the screen it needs
   (small or large) and the length of one session (minutes).
2. Choose the device class where it works best, and give one reason.

*Your result:* the three facts, the device class and the reason.

::: {.check}
A good answer names the input (touch, buttons, keyboard), the screen (small
or large) and a session length, then one device class with a reason that
uses them, for example "a 5-minute puzzle game with touch: a smartphone,
because it is played anywhere in short sessions".
:::
:::

## Case study: Tap Runner

*Tap Runner* is a made-up endless running game. The character runs by itself,
and the player taps to jump over blocks. The game shows 60 frames per second
and saves the best distance. The studio releases it on Android phones, on
iPhones and on Windows PCs, with one build for each. The test phone has a CPU
core at 2.4 GHz and 4 GB of RAM. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson
uses this game; play it with the Tap Runner mini-game of section 1.2 (scan its
QR code).

## Further reading

Tanenbaum and Austin, *Structured Computer Organization*, 6th ed., Chapter 1
("Introduction"): languages, levels and virtual machines, and the "computer
zoo".

## Exercises

1. Name the four jobs of a computing system. Give an example of each in a
   racing game.
2. Why can one phone run thousands of different games?
3. A phone has 6 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. A player installs ten big
   games. Which one fills up? Which one fills up when the player keeps five
   games open?
4. Name the three steps of the instruction cycle.
5. What does "3 GHz" tell you about a processor core?
6. Name the four parts of a digital platform.
7. Why does a game need one build for Android phones and another build for
   Windows PCs?
8. Why must an Android game be tested on many phones?
9. A game needs a gamepad and a TV and is played for two hours. Which device
   class fits it best?
10. Name two things that change when a phone game moves to a console.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Input: steering with the touch screen; processing: computing the car's movement; output: the picture and the engine sound; storage: saving the best lap time.
2. The program is stored in memory like data, so a new game only needs to be loaded into memory.
3. Installing fills the storage (128 GB). Keeping games open fills the RAM (6 GB).
4. Fetch, decode, execute.
5. How fast one core works: 3 billion clock ticks per second.
6. A family of devices, an operating system, development tools, and a store with its rules.
7. The platforms are different (system, store, and the processor: ARM in phones, x86 in most PCs), so the engine makes a separate build for each.
8. Android runs on thousands of phone models with different processors and screens.
9. A console.
10. For example the input (gamepad instead of touch) and the screen layout (a large TV).
:::
